examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential diagnosis for this woman's bruising and bleeding, and how you would distinguish between them.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with mucocutaneous bleeding suggests a primary haemostatic disorder. Top of the list is ITP given the post-viral trigger, isolated platelet drop with normal smear and coagulation, and no organomegaly. TTP is excluded by normal LDH/haptoglobin and no schistocytes or neurological signs. HIV-associated thrombocytopenia is excluded by a negative HIV test. Drug-induced thrombocytopenia is excluded by no new medication exposure. Marrow infiltration/leukaemia is excluded by normal white cell count, no blasts, and no organomegaly. SLE-associated thrombocytopenia is unlikely given a negative ANA and no other lupus features.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants ranked reasoning linking each differential to specific case findings, not just a list of names.

examinerBank.question: What is the pathophysiological mechanism underlying the platelet destruction in ITP?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Autoantibodies, typically IgG, target platelet surface glycoproteins such as GPIIb/IIIa or GPIb/IX. Opsonised platelets are then prematurely removed by Fc-receptor-mediated phagocytosis in the spleen and liver. Megakaryocytes can also be targeted, impairing compensatory platelet production, so destruction outpaces production. A preceding viral illness can trigger this through molecular mimicry or immune complex formation.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants antibody-mediated destruction mechanism with mention of Fc-receptor phagocytosis and the production/destruction mismatch; bonus for molecular mimicry link to preceding illness.

examinerBank.question: Why would you not routinely perform a bone marrow aspirate in this patient before starting treatment?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: In a young patient with a typical presentation — isolated thrombocytopenia, normal white cell count and differential, no blasts on smear, no organomegaly — ITP is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion supported by peripheral blood findings. Bone marrow aspirate is reserved for atypical features, age over 60, failure to respond to first-line therapy, or before splenectomy, not for routine confirmation.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests understanding that ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion and marrow biopsy is not mandatory in typical young patients.

examinerBank.question: Why is platelet transfusion generally avoided as first-line treatment in ITP, and when would you use it?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Transfused platelets are subject to the same autoantibody-mediated destruction as the patient's own platelets, so the increment is often minimal and short-lived. It is reserved for life-threatening bleeding such as intracranial haemorrhage or severe uncontrolled bleeding, usually given alongside IVIG and high-dose corticosteroids to try to achieve a more durable rise.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants explanation of the mechanism (antibody targets transfused platelets too) plus correct indication for use in emergencies only.

examinerBank.question: How do you clinically distinguish petechiae/purpura due to thrombocytopenia from palpable purpura of vasculitis?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Thrombocytopenic petechiae and purpura are non-palpable, flat, and non-blanching, reflecting passive extravasation of red cells through capillaries due to failure of the primary platelet plug. Palpable purpura, as seen in vasculitis (e.g. Henoch-Schönlein purpura, ANCA-associated vasculitis), is raised and firm because it results from inflammatory vessel wall damage and true vasculitic infiltration, not simple failure of platelet plugging.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the palpable-versus-non-palpable distinction with the underlying mechanistic reasoning, not just a description.

framework: bruising/bleeding tendency → confirm low platelets → classify by mechanism (production vs destruction vs consumption) → screen for driving/underlying cause → confirm isolated thrombocytopenia → treat per severity

patient.personality: anxious, talkative when nervous, keeps pointing at her bruises and asking if she has 'blood cancer'
patient.openingLine: Doctor, I woke up covered in bruises and my gums won't stop bleeding when I brush my teeth — please tell me it's not something serious.

Gum bleeding when brushing teeth for the past 2 days, plus a nosebleed yesterday that took 15 minutes to stop
Noticed tiny red-purple pinpoint spots on her shins and forearms, like a rash that doesn't fade or itch
Her period started 4 days ago and is much heavier than usual, soaking pads every 1-2 hours
Had a bad flu-like illness with fever and sore throat about 2 weeks before the bruising started, which resolved on its own
No weight loss, no night sweats, no fevers currently, appetite normal

examination.general: Alert, anxious-looking young woman, well-nourished, no pallor, no jaundice, no lymphadenopathy. Multiple scattered ecchymoses of varying sizes on both forearms and shins. Petechiae noted on the anterior shins and hard palate.
examination.cardio: Normal heart sounds, no murmurs, no signs of anaemia-related flow murmur
examination.abdo: Soft, non-tender, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly palpable
examination.neuro: Alert and orientated, no focal deficit, no signs of intracranial bleed (no headache, no altered consciousness, no focal weakness)

investigations.name: Full blood count
investigations.result: Hb 12.6 g/dL, WCC 6.8 x10^9/L (normal differential), Platelets 8 x10^9/L (isolated severe thrombocytopenia), MCV 88 fL

investigations.name: Peripheral blood smear
investigations.result: Markedly reduced platelet numbers, occasional large platelets seen; no schistocytes, no blasts, red cells and white cells morphologically normal

investigations.name: LDH and haptoglobin
investigations.result: LDH normal, haptoglobin normal (argues against microangiopathic haemolysis/TTP)

investigations.name: Bone marrow aspirate/trephine
investigations.result: Not performed — reserved for atypical features, age >60, or failure to respond to first-line therapy; not indicated in this typical presentation

pathophys.petechiae and mucocutaneous bruising: Severe thrombocytopenia (<20-30 x10^9/L) impairs primary haemostatic plug formation at sites of minor capillary trauma; small vessels leak red cells into the dermis producing non-blanching pinpoint petechiae and larger ecchymoses, in contrast to the deep muscle/joint bleeds of coagulation factor disorders
pathophys.gum bleeding and epistaxis: Mucosal surfaces are especially vulnerable because of constant minor mechanical trauma (brushing, sneezing) combined with a rich superficial capillary network reliant on platelet plug formation for haemostasis
pathophys.menorrhagia: Endometrial spiral artery bleeding at menstruation is normally controlled by platelet plug formation and vasoconstriction; profound thrombocytopenia removes this primary haemostatic mechanism, producing prolonged heavy flow
pathophys.isolated thrombocytopenia (mechanism of: Autoantibodies (typically IgG) directed against platelet surface glycoproteins (GPIIb/IIIa, GPIb/IX) opsonise platelets, which are then phagocytosed prematurely by splenic and hepatic macrophages via Fc receptors; megakaryocytes may also be antibody-targeted, impairing compensatory platelet production — production fails to match accelerated peripheral destruction
pathophys.post-viral trigger: Molecular mimicry between viral antigens and platelet glycoproteins, or immune complex deposition on platelet membranes following a preceding viral illness, triggers the autoantibody response typical of acute ITP, especially in younger patients

staging: Severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count <10 x10^9/L) with active mucocutaneous bleeding — high bleeding-risk category requiring treatment rather than observation alone; newly diagnosed ITP (within 3 months of diagnosis, not yet classified as persistent or chronic)

immediate: Assess bleeding severity (mucocutaneous only vs internal/CNS bleeding) — this patient has no critical bleeding
Admit for observation given platelet count <10 x10^9/L with active bleeding
Avoid IM injections, NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants
Group and save; platelet transfusion reserved ONLY for life-threatening bleeding (platelets are rapidly destroyed by circulating antibody, so transfusion is not first-line therapy)
definitive: First-line: oral corticosteroids — prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (or dexamethasone 40 mg/day x4 days as alternative pulsed regimen)
IVIG (1 g/kg single dose or over 2 days) if rapid platelet rise needed (active significant bleeding, pre-procedure) or steroids contraindicated
Second-line (steroid-refractory/relapse): splenectomy, rituximab, or thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag/romiplostim) — specialist haematology referral
supportive: Bleeding precautions counselling: avoid contact sports, razors, NSAIDs/aspirin
Contraceptive/menstrual management referral if menorrhagia is significant (tranexamic acid can be considered, hormonal options with gynaecology)
Patient education on recognising warning signs of serious bleeding (headache, visual change, confusion — suggesting intracranial haemorrhage)
followUp: Repeat FBC within 48-72 hours of starting steroids to confirm platelet response
Taper steroids once platelet count recovers to safe levels (>30-50 x10^9/L) and stable
Haematology follow-up to monitor for chronic/relapsing ITP (persisting beyond 12 months)
Re-screen for secondary causes (HIV, hepatitis, autoimmune disease) if atypical course or poor response to first-line therapy

stationChecklist.item: Characterises the bleeding pattern (bruising, petechiae, mucosal bleeding sites, duration, spontaneity)
stationChecklist.answer: 3-day history of spontaneous bruising, gum bleeding, epistaxis, petechiae, heavy menses — mucocutaneous pattern
stationChecklist.why: Mucocutaneous bleeding pattern points to platelet/primary haemostatic disorder rather than coagulation factor deficiency

stationChecklist.item: Asks about a preceding viral illness or infection in the weeks before onset
stationChecklist.answer: Flu-like illness with fever and sore throat 2 weeks prior, self-resolved
stationChecklist.why: Classic trigger for acute post-viral ITP, especially in young patients

stationChecklist.item: Screens for constitutional/systemic symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fevers, bone pain, fatigue)
stationChecklist.why: Absence argues against marrow infiltration, lymphoma, or TB as the underlying driver
HIV-associated thrombocytopenia is a key differential in KZN and must always be screened for

stationChecklist.item: Takes a thorough medication history including NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants, new drugs/antibiotics
stationChecklist.answer: No regular medication, no NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants, no new drugs
stationChecklist.why: Excludes drug-induced thrombocytopenia as an alternative diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Screens for autoimmune disease features (joint pains, rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers)
Examines skin and mucosa for petechiae, ecchymoses, and distinguishes from palpable purpura
stationChecklist.answer: Non-blanching petechiae on shins and hard palate; ecchymoses at various stages; no palpable purpura
stationChecklist.why: Non-palpable petechiae confirm a platelet-mediated bleeding disorder, not vasculitis
Absence supports isolated ITP over lymphoma/leukaemia/chronic liver disease

stationChecklist.item: Generates a ranked differential distinguishing ITP from TTP, HIV-associated, drug-induced, and marrow infiltrative causes with linked reasoning
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning is the exam philosophy — thrombocytopenia has a broad differential requiring systematic exclusion

stationChecklist.item: Requests FBC with smear, coagulation screen, HIV test, and considers ANA/DAT as indicated
stationChecklist.answer: Isolated thrombocytopenia (8 x10^9/L), normal smear (no schistocytes/blasts), normal coagulation, HIV negative
stationChecklist.why: Confirms isolated thrombocytopenia and excludes TTP, coagulopathy, and secondary causes — the core confirmatory pathway for a diagnosis of exclusion

stationChecklist.item: Recognises bone marrow aspirate is NOT routinely required in typical presentations
stationChecklist.answer: Reserved for atypical features, age >60, or treatment failure
stationChecklist.why: Avoids unnecessary invasive testing in a straightforward case

stationChecklist.item: Assesses bleeding severity to guide urgency of treatment and admission decision
stationChecklist.answer: Platelet <10 with active mucosal bleeding warrants admission and treatment, not observation alone
stationChecklist.why: Bleeding risk stratification determines whether to treat, observe, or transfuse

stationChecklist.item: Outlines first-line treatment (corticosteroids +/- IVIG) and explains why platelet transfusion is not first-line
stationChecklist.answer: Prednisone 1mg/kg/day or dexamethasone pulse; IVIG if rapid response needed; platelet transfusion reserved for life-threatening bleeding as transfused platelets are also destroyed
stationChecklist.why: Core management reasoning per SA haematology practice
